title: PearlClear
question: How does an oyster make a pearl?
hook: Forget the grain of sand. A pearl starts when a few shell-making cells end up in the wrong place, then grows thousands of layers each thinner than a bacterium. Open an oyster, grow a pearl, and see why it shines.

explainer.title: A shell-making skin
explainer.text: A pearl oyster is a soft animal between two hinged shells. Lining them is the mantle, a sheet of tissue whose outer cells build the shell: an organic skin, a layer of prisms, then on the inside layer after layer of nacre, or mother-of-pearl. A pearl is made of the same nacre by the same kind of cell.

explainer.title: Not a grain of sand
explainer.text: Sand rarely starts a pearl. Grit between the mantle and the shell is usually flushed out, or coated onto the shell as a blister. A loose pearl needs mantle cells inside the soft tissue. A burrowing parasite or an injury can drag a few in. They multiply into a pocket, the pearl sac, and coat whatever is inside with nacre.

explainer.title: Bricks and mortar
explainer.text: Nacre is a wall of flat aragonite tablets, about half a micrometre thick and 5 to 8 micrometres wide, glued by organic mortar 10 to 30 nanometres thick. One pearl imaged in full detail held 2,615 layers laid over 548 days, four or five a day. Growth rates vary with species and water.

explainer.title: Why it is tough
explainer.text: Plain aragonite is brittle as chalk. In nacre a crack has to zigzag through the mortar around each tablet, and the tablets slide and grip as it goes. Nacre can absorb up to about a thousand times more energy before breaking than the pure mineral, so engineers copy its design.

explainer.title: Colour from layers
explainer.text: Each boundary between tablet and mortar reflects a little light. Where the extra trip between layers is a whole number of wavelengths, the reflections add up. That is thin-film interference repeated hundreds of times. Tilt a pearl and the colour shifts. Pigment gives the body colour, and interference gives the overtone.

explainer.title: A bead and a scrap of skin
explainer.text: Kokichi and Ume Mikimoto grew half-pearls in 1893. Tatsuhei Mise patented round cultured pearls in 1907, and Tokichi Nishikawa filed for the same method. A technician slips a shell bead and a square of donor mantle into a living oyster. The cells grow round the bead and coat it in nacre over months or years.

concepts.def: The sheet of tissue that lines a mollusc's shell. Its outer epithelial cells secrete the shell and pearls.
Mother-of-pearl: the iridescent inner layer of many shells and the material of pearls, made of aragonite tablets and organic mortar.
A crystal form of calcium carbonate. Nacre tablets are made of it.
A closed pocket of mantle epithelial cells inside the tissue that lays nacre inward. Every pearl grows in one.
Nacre grown onto the inside of the shell over an intruder. It is part of the shell, not a loose pearl.
The thin film of proteins and chitin, 10 to 30 nanometres thick, that glues nacre's tablets together.
Reflections from the top and bottom of thin layers that add up for some colours and cancel for others.
Lustre is how bright and sharp a pearl's reflections are. Overtone is a colour that seems to float over its body colour.
A real nacre pearl grown with human help, usually from a shell bead and a square of donor mantle.
Placing a bead and a mantle graft in an oyster's gonad: the basis of round pearl culture since the 1900s.
